does this redfish client support talking to multiple SMCs at the same time?
Yes.

If you're addressing a specific SMC communication issue, a daemon might be effective. However, for the broader challenge of REST/HTTPs/Redfish communication, it seems to add unnecessary complexity and reduces flexibility. Relying on a single application for all communications introduces a single point of failure. Additionally, the need for type-safe classes for Redfish schemas may stem from this added layer of indirection between the application and server. The two reasons you mentioned for a Redfish client daemon—reusability and security—are already addressed in the industry through HTTP libraries, OpenSSL, and various server-specific authentication and authorization methods.

1. This design/daemon is concentrating on enabling BMC to be able to communicate with SMCs that specifically can only talks Redfish, and has no intention for solving the broader challenge of REST/HTTPs/Redfish communication.
2. Single point of failure also means single point of optimization/fix and no duplicated code, which is a reasonable tradeoff in this case as failure to communicating with SMCs is not something completely unacceptable.
3. The client and server are still going to be communicate via Redfish directly, the type-safe classes are just client implementation detail of how to process response and construct request regarding Redfish protocol. It is a common and good practice to wrap complex raw json objects with classes, and the codegen lib will save engineer time for manually writing those classes. In terms of flexibility, even though I don't believe that's a must-have or high priority feature, the lib itself should have enough room for making change and improvement.
4. The proposal daemon will definitely use some HTTP libraries that can provide
industry standard security feature and may apply SMC specific authentication and
authorization methods if any. The reason that security is being mentioned in the design is purely a comparison to "redfish aggregation", which exposing the SMC
directly onto the external network. HTTP layer security won't solve this problem as we would like the SMC to be completely invisible to external other than the BMC.
Done

> and has no intention for solving the broader challenge of REST/HTTPs/Redfish communication.

So we're duplicating a lot of code?  Unclear how that scales in this design.

This looks like it got marked done without really answering the overall question (which I had the same question below).  This design is proposing we do redfish parsing in more than one repository, whereas previously there was only one (bmcweb).  How do we make sure we're not duplicating a lot of code between them, and thereby requiring all redfish features be added twice, once to the aggregator and once to this client?

> Single point of failure

Not sure I agree the tradeoff is reasonable, and single point of failure implies that we can't create new applications with shared code, rather than rewriting.  Please reword.  FWIW, the reason this wasn't rolled out into its own application for redfish aggregation is so that connections could be persistent, queued, and shared, so as not to overwhelm the Redfish server.  There's certainly a tradeoff here to discuss, but it needs discussed in the background section.

> common and good practice

Is there any other Redfish client that's done this?  As someone who has tried and failed several times, I wasn't aware of any that are used at any kind of scale.  Others have tried (links below) and ended up having to fall back to normal HTTP.  I thought even the guys doing grpc rack manager had fallen back to passing around raw json objects and binary blobs because of the inconsistencies in the Redfish type system.

As much as I really want to see this succeed, I'm worried we're going to solve 80% of the problem, then not have the ability to solve the last 20%
to make a complete solution.

https://github.com/Nordix/go-redfish
https://gbmc.googlesource.com/gbmcweb/+/refs/heads/master

@Xinyuan. 
"I’m unclear about the purpose of the Redfish client service since no other service depends on it. My assumption is that other BMC services use it for external communications.

While a single point of failure can streamline optimization and reduce code duplication, achieving this doesn’t require a single service. A library can provide the same benefits without introducing a single point of failure. If a service using the library fails, only that service is affected, and other HTTP services remain operational.

By replacing the DBus calls to the Redfish client service with HTTP library calls, any service can directly communicate with external SMCs."

> This design is proposing we do redfish parsing in more than one repository, whereas previously there was only one (bmcweb)

From my quick scan of the [redfish_aggregator](https://github.com/openbmc/bmcweb/blob/master/redfish-core/include/redfish_aggregator.hpp#L862-L906) code, I don't see it does any parsing of the redfish response to proper cpp class, but just basic json parsing, and it purely forwards the json with additional prefix as response.

> A library can provide the same benefits without introducing a single point of failure.

Not sure I agree with that. If there is a bug in the library that causes failure, every single caller using this library will hit the same failure, not a big difference than having a single service. If the failure root cause is not in the common code path but feature dependent code path, then the failure of one feature should not affect the others if we are able to properly isolate them within the service. At the extreme cases we can always span one process per feature/task to achieve the complete isolation.

> By replacing the DBus calls to the Redfish client service with HTTP library calls, any service can directly communicate with external SMCs

Some BMC services may not do DBus call but wait for Dbus signal and act upon, so they do not directly communicate with external SMCs. They rely on some other daemon or service to talk to the SMCs and emit the dbus signal it's expected. This is one of the main purpose of this design is to provide such service/daemon.

In terms of HTTP library, I am actually happy to adopt it within the daemon once it is being merged upstream and have good enough feature parity.
Done
Does this redfish client supports redfish event listener as well?
Not in the current plan, might support such feature in the future.
how does task maintain this internal state, can you please elaborate?

Each task will maintain its own state in memory in some cpp struct and will be updated in every poll to the SMC. The state would mainly contain the result of the last poll (likely a map or vector of cpp object that corresponds to the exposed D-Bus object by leveraging the `sdbusplus` lib), as well as value needed for task execution such as last poll time.

how does read/write error handling done in this redfish client.

does this redfish-client support re-try mechanisms?

Re-try should be supported. Error handling would be case by case depending on the feature. For example in sensor monitoring, if the SMC isn't available, the client would marked the monitored sensor as unavailable and probably emit a Event Log. Both retry and error handling should be configurable individually for each task by the configuration files to some extend.
any other BMC can act as SMC here right?
Theoretically any device that accept Redfish protocol and can be reached by the host BMC can be the target SMC for this redfish client.

Overall, I don't really see a design here.  I see a lot of thoughts that neglect that this component needs to interact with:
1. DMTF - As the publish new schemas and develop new features.  Some of these are unavailable for 6 months after merge, how is that handled if schemas are static?
2. Implementations of Redfish that are under development, and might not have complete schemas, as well as implementations of Redfish that are not OpenBMC.
3. OpenBMC as a whole, which has a lot of the component pieces for this already built and proven, and has OEM schemas that already exist and have history (are those supported?).
4. Implementations of HTTP/JSON/core libraries that will be extended with new features over time.

There are lots of unanswered questions surrounding those things in this design, and the wording (maybe unintentional) makes it sound like this effort is just going to rewrite everything because DMTF/Curl/Beast/Nlohmann/bmcweb http_client don't work, but fails to specify why.  If that's not the intent, lets get that written down what core components we plan on using.

Overall, I think the right path here is to start implementing the redfish->struct conversion in a gerrit review (ideally starting with the DMTF one as a base), and lets look at the generated code to see if it's something that will work.  Ideally please start with an old redfish schema, and show that new redfish schemas can be parsed without re-compiling the library against the new schemas (for at least the properties that existed at the time).  As much as I dislike it, this is a requirement that the Redfish standard places on client implementations.

The other elephant in the room is that the implementation here needs to be capable of supporting schemas that aren't published, or are only published on the systems that produce them, and duplicating those schemas to OpenBMC would violate copyrights (ie, Redfish supports more than just OpenBMC).  FWIW, I think this somewhat necessitates moving away from a compile time struct generation, and more toward Redpath, which in DTMF is intended to be the solution to this exact problem, but wasn't really mentioned in the background.  If Redpath doesn't work for this use case, ideally some feedback to DMTF is in order.

> DMTF - As the publish new schemas and develop new features. Some of these are unavailable for 6 months after merge, how is that handled if schemas are static?

The client here will depend on the schemas, similar to how bmcweb depends on the schemas.  As new versions are released, the dependency will be updated.

SMCs might be running old versions.  The project will support old versions for a set amount of time and the client will be responsible for being backwards compatible (during that deprecation window).  We need to update this design document to specify the time window for backwards compatibility.

Schemas are always backwards compatible; the only issue with backwards compatibility is when the BMC redfish client requires properties (or methods or whole schemas) that are only available in latest revisions.  This is the part that we will have a documented policy on timeliness.

bmcweb historically hasn't used schemas for code generation.  It does use the registries, but those are also checked in so it's easy to apply WIP DMTF changes to builds.

> We need to update this design document to specify the time window for backwards compatibility.

Definitely worth documenting what compatibility means here.  For example, Thermal/Power schemas are still "supported" by the standard, even if they might not be recommended, so would we deprecate those today?  Doesn't really need an answer, but at least some idealized goals here would be good to add.

>  the only issue with backwards compatibility is when the BMC redfish client requires properties (or methods or whole schemas) that are only available in latest revisions.

Or if the SMC updates to a newer version than is available to the client, and we don't design the parser to handle that condition (new versions of existing schemas)

> code generation.

I should clarify, recently code was added for generating enums, but there's no architectural requirement that it be used, fallback to non schema defined structs is still available in code.


BTW, if we can make this work, I fully support it, but specs like Redpath exist because there's a lot of corner cases with typesafe schemas on Redfish that are difficult to handle in a design.

Adding code generation for redfish schema is useful only if it stands as a compile time contract between two services. But in this case it seems the only consumer of the generated class is redfish client service. The other end of consumer may not be even writtern in c++. I don't see any value in creating one more level of tooling side indirection . It just add to the development complexity instead. If some one really want to have type safe classes for json serialisation , it is already supported by nlohmann(https://github.com/nlohmann/json) . All you have to do is just add NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_NON_INTRUSIVE to your application classes.

> First approach is to direct json access:

The example given here:
1. Doesn't follow best practices (we'd generally not use contains and operator[] in proximity)  we'd use find), and even that isn't best practice.  In practice, the helper functions in bmcweb we have now use a loop because it's faster/generates less code.
2. Doesn't handle errors.  This is an important part of what we're talking about: How does this function if the schemas don't match in expected ways?  I see a couple exceptions thrown, but obviously a redfish client can't just crash when it sees an unexpected schema, so examples of error handling are important here.
3. As Abhilash points out, can already be done with nlohmann::json directly.
4. Doesn't implement Redfish schemas correctly.  Each property can be represented in Redfish as null, or return an expected error (something like retry-after) code from the backend.  Those don't seem to be represented in the backend.  Redfish clients have to handle the following states:
5. Has no checking of @odata.id

1. Value filled in with the appropriate type
2. Value is null
3. Value is filled in with the wrong type (this would be a bad implementation of redfish, but happens in practice).
4. Value is not present.
5. Value parent key is not present.
6. Value is correct per redfish, but not representable in the struct (uint > 64 bit for example)

Each of these (with the possible exception of 5, because it could be combined with 4) needs to have some representation in the type safe struct.

These are the kinds of things that need called out in this design requirements.

> There is an alternative approach

To be clear, this is essentially a copy of what bmcweb does for reading redfish parameters.  Please check out readJson for how it's currently solved.  If it needs to be extended for this use case, it could be, but doesn't necessarily need to be.  To be clear, readJson as it exists today is imperfect for this use case, but does handle errors correctly.
Apologies..... The markdown combined my two numbered lists and renumbered them, making that really confusing.  Starting at #5 was supposed to be a new list.  I would edit it if I could.

It seems to me the concerning points can be summarized as the following points:
1. naming convention: we will keep the generated code reflects the redfish schema as much as possible and people can actually examine the generated code directly to find the needed property/metadata etc.
2. code editors support: seems to be a minor concern but there is definitely a doable way to improve it in the future if necessary
3. memory and performance problem: I don't think there will be much overhead for memory and performance
4. error handling: as I mentioned in other comment and also added to the design doc, the generated data class will be able to capture expected error into "error" field and unexpected error/key/value into "leftover" field so that the caller can decide what to do with it

I also want to emphasize that the generated code primarily consists of data classes designed to encapsulate Redfish JSON responses. These classes expose both valid and invalid data, as well as any associated errors. The responsibility for handling this data and determining the appropriate logic lies with the caller. As such, this library is intended to be lightweight and focused, rather than a comprehensive solution for the broader spectrum of Redfish-related challenges.

Generated types should be placed within schema-specific namespaces to prevent collisions, even if it makes the code slightly more verbose. Using std::optional or std::expected for wrapping errors and optional data serialization can result in a modern C++ style, though this might be a subjective preference.
 
C++ Templates can already generate such code, so why create another tool for the same purpose? When comparing the usage on the call side, there may not be any significant advantage to using tool-generated code.

It’s better to compare the call-side code, including error handling, for both the generated code and a JSON serializer approach like the one used in bmcweb before making a decision.

> Generated types should be placed within schema-specific namespaces to prevent collisions, even if it makes the code slightly more verbose. Using std::optional or std::expected for wrapping errors and optional data serialization can result in a modern C++ style, though this might be a subjective preference.

Yes, this is exactly what the codegen would likely do.

> C++ Templates can already generate such code

I don't think C++ template can generate code based on json schema?

> I also want to emphasize that the generated code primarily consists of data classes designed to encapsulate Redfish JSON responses. These classes expose both valid and invalid data, as well as any associated errors

This design doc doesn't say that, and doesn't give examples;  That's part of the confusion.

how does the daemon handle discovery of new objects created by the SatMC ? example - if the SatMC is creating new log entries at run time then would the daemon periodically poll for for entries and populate them over dbus ?

Yes, as mentioned in the later design, the daemon will periodically poll the SMC to either get an up-to-date value of existing entries and update the corresponding properties on dbus (likely in sensor monitoring use case), or get new entries and populate them over dbus (likely in event log collection use case).
Done

Can we add requirements around implementing the redfish protocol to the specification, rather than whatever flavor the device you're working on happens to implement?  If we're not implementing a Redfish client to the standard, and are only operating on the bmcweb "flavor" there's a lot of far simpler designs here (see dbus-rest).

The "flavor" really depends on the Redfish implementation of the SMC, not that the client can decide, so the design should make the daemon as lightweight and flexible as possible, and move "flavor" to config as much as possible so that different machine can just have different config and call it good. Take sensor monitoring for example, the daemon will need to get Redfish [Sensor](https://www.dmtf.org/sites/default/files/standards/documents/DSP0268_2024.3.html#sensor-1101) from the redfish response, but which exact redfish path to get it and how exactly it is supposed to map to a dbus sensor would live in the config if possible. (some common mapping may still live within the Cpp code).
Done

does the config file allows picking the features. Example - I would like the daemon to do event log collection but not to do the sensor monitoring (the platform could have a different way to achieve this performance reasons.)

Yes, that is the plan. For example, if we want the daemon to do event log collection, an "eventLogCollection" config would need to be created. If later we want the daemon to do sensor monitoring, a "sensorMonitoring" config should be added. Also, if we want to do event log collection towards a different SMC, another "eventLogCollection" config needs to be added with different target SMC.
Done
Can we call this "hostname" please?  URLs are governed by the redfish standard, so a config file shouldn't have URLs in it.

This is not hostname but the exact redfish URLs. For example, if we need sensorX from the SMC and the url to get it is `http://201.65.75.135/redfish/v1/Chassis/10/Sensors/55` then the config should contains something like ` {"sensorX": "Chassis/10/Sensors/55"}`, and the daemon would do the polling on this exact url to retrieve the sensor data.
Done

I think what you described as a "network library that supports both TCP and HTTP" operates at a different layer than what this Redfish client design addresses. The primary purpose of this design is to enable discovering and retrieving resources from the HMC via Redfish and making them available to other services running on the BMC through D-Bus. The heavy lifting is specific to: how to discover the HMC IP/port, what Redfish queries to make for different resources, how to parse and transform Redfish responses into their D-Bus equivalents, and how to handle concerns like log deduplication and firmware update orchestration.

How the HTTP requests are made is a small, encapsulated part of this daemon. In our downstream implementation, only **406 lines (13%)** are dedicated to HTTP networking, while the remaining **2,684 lines (87%)** implement the core business logic described above. The HTTP layer is intentionally thin and could be backed by libcurl, Boost.Beast, a shared networking library, or even a simple `curl` subprocess. The choice has minimal impact on the overall design.

> Once we have a common TCP + HTTP client layer in place, implementing a Redfish client on top of it becomes straightforward.

This understates the actual complexity. The referenced example ([reactor/redfish.cpp](https://github.com/abhilashraju/reactor/blob/main/examples/redfish/redfish.cpp#L203)) demonstrates making HTTP calls, but a production Redfish client requires far more than that: schema aware response parsing, mapping diverse Redfish resource types to D-Bus interfaces, persistent deduplication of log entries across polling cycles, multi step firmware update workflows with task tracking, and sensor lifecycle management. None of which are simplified by having a better HTTP library.

That said, I fully agree that a reusable, well optimized networking stack would be valuable for the broader ecosystem. However, that should be pursued as a separate, standalone effort. The Redfish client's HTTP layer is already cleanly isolated behind a simple interface, so migrating it to use a shared networking library in the future would be straightforward and low risk. It would not require any changes to the core business logic.

Added an Extensibility section to the design.
```
The design is not tied to any specific SMC vendor or limited to only mentioned
resources. Throughout this document, the Nvidia HMC is used for illustration
purposes, but the design supports any Redfish-compliant device. Extensibility is
achieved by the following mechanisms:

- **Multi-device support**: Multiple configuration files can be activated
  simultaneously, each targeting a different satellite controller. A single BMC
  can communicate with multiple SMCs of different vendors concurrently.
  Supporting a new vendor requires only a new configuration file; no daemon
  code changes are needed as long as the device exposes standard Redfish
  resources.
- **New resource types**: Each resource type is an independent task with its own
  configuration, collection logic, and D-Bus transformation. New resource types
  can be added without modifying existing tasks.
- **Configurable transformation**: The `Mappers` mechanism allows per-platform
  customization of how Redfish resources are mapped to D-Bus objects, decoupling
  the SMC's Redfish schema from the BMC's D-Bus representation.
```
Regarding your example, the design already supports querying attributes across multiple satellite BMCs as each SMC's IP is defined in its SatelliteController object exposed by entity-manager, and multiple configurations can be activated simultaneously to target different controllers. And again, the design is not limited to SMCs but should be working with any Redfish-compliant device as Patrick mentioned above.
